investigation.title: Burning and Suppression of Solids - II
investigation.objective: BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth.

crew_environments.justification: Flown on the ISS; Nomex was tested because it is heavily used aboard the ISS as a fire barrier (report p. 54).
Aims to find the worst case for material flammability in spacecraft environments and compare it with the NASA-STD-6001 upward test (report p. 11).

evidence.text: Find the minimum O2 or flow at which a material burns in space; helps engineers select the safest materials.
evidence.source: BASS-II_Summary_Report.pdf (NASA/TM-20210011385, 2021) p. 11; PSI-25 metadata (i_Investigation.txt) Research Impacts

evidence.text: Flame growth rates studied to see how quickly a fire in space can grow and whether flames reach a finite size.
Results feed models used to design fire detection and suppression systems; flows reduced until flames quenched.
Flammability boundary for PMMA rods; minimum about 13.5% O2.
Opposed and concurrent flame spread rates over films, slabs, rods and fabric.
Quenching and blowoff extinction limits as a function of O2 and flow.
Combustion products (O2, CO, CO2), heat release rate, global equivalence ratio.

fuel.geometry: Flat films and slabs (1- and 2-sided), cylindrical rods, fabric sheets, spherical sections

evidence.text: Calibrated initial O2 13.6-22.2% across 129 tests
ISS cabin pressure; analyses use P = 1 atm. Not recorded per test.
Fan-driven duct flow up to ~55 cm/s (no restrictors) or ~35 cm/s (two restrictors); per-test values are free text.
Flight platform: International Space Station
Spread rate of the leading edge, e.g. steady 2.2 mm/s over 100 um PMMA film.
Quenching flow speeds and blowoff limits vs O2.
Flame length, width and standoff distance over time.
Rod regression and mass burning rate along the flammability boundary.

computed_findings.finding: Initial O2 ranged 13.6-22.2% (reduced by N2 dilution from ISS air); most tests were below 19% O2.
computed_findings.method: Calibrated initial O2 column; values outside 10-25% excluded.

computed_findings.finding: Lowest-O2 tests were almost all PMMA rods; one sample failed to ignite at 13.6% O2, while flames ignited higher survived down to final readings of about 13.6%.
Final CO in the 250 L glovebox reached up to 950 ppm (sensor over range in some tests); thick PMMA and rods gave the highest values.
Many tests deliberately ran the flow down to extinction to map limits; blowoff and no-ignition outcomes were also recorded.
computed_findings.method: Keywords ('ext', 'blowoff', 'no ign', 'would not stay lit') in fan/air display text. Text was transcribed, so counts are approximate.

key_findings.finding: Flame spread over black PMMA rods was seen down to 17.5% O2 in microgravity, while in normal gravity it was not seen below 19%.
key_findings.fire_safety_relevance: Low ventilation in space can let materials burn at O2 levels where Earth tests show no spread.

evidence.text: Comparison of minimum O2 for flame spread

key_findings.finding: The PMMA rod flammability boundary has a minimum near 13.5% O2, well below the 15.4% upward-burning limit measured in normal gravity.
key_findings.fire_safety_relevance: The standard Earth upward test may not be conservative for space; the low-flow 'Goldilocks' zone is typical of spacecraft ventilation near surfaces.

evidence.text: Flammability boundary minimum and comparison with 1g limit

key_findings.finding: Extrapolating the blowoff limit to zero flow gives a conservative estimate of the minimum O2 for material flammability in space.
key_findings.fire_safety_relevance: Proposed method to derate materials from normal-gravity tests so they will not burn in space.

evidence.text: Blowoff branch is linear with flow

key_findings.finding: Ignition delay near the limit can be almost 10 times the NASA-STD-6001 igniter on-time, and ignition limits sit at higher O2 than flammability limits.
key_findings.fire_safety_relevance: A material that fails to ignite in a standard test may still sustain a flame once lit by a longer heat source.

evidence.text: Olson conclusions

key_findings.finding: Thin PMMA flames went out by radiative extinction at opposed flows of about 1 cm/s (100-300 um) and 1.5 cm/s (400 um); the critical velocity was about 10 mm/s at 21% O2 and 30 mm/s at 16%.
key_findings.fire_safety_relevance: Cutting ventilation can extinguish flames on thin materials; less flow is needed to sustain them at higher O2.

evidence.text: Bhattacharjee results, Table 2.1

key_findings.finding: Concurrent-flow quenching speeds for SIBAL fabric were 1-5 cm/s, higher at lower O2 (O2 varied 21% to 16%).
key_findings.fire_safety_relevance: Defines the ventilation level below which fabric fires quench on their own.

evidence.text: T'ien abstract

key_findings.finding: Nomex samples did not ignite; a wax candle ejected a burning droplet upstream.
key_findings.fire_safety_relevance: Supports Nomex as an ISS fire barrier; melting plastics can spread fire by ejecting burning droplets in microgravity.

evidence.text: Ferkul results

key_findings.finding: Flames were fuel rich (global equivalence ratio about 1.3) with high CO/CO2 ratios; heat release was mostly well below 100 W.
key_findings.fire_safety_relevance: Small space fires are inefficient and produce relatively more CO; a fire this size would dilute to about 1.5 ppm CO in the US Lab, below the 10 ppm long-term SMAC.

evidence.text: Overall conclusions and combustion products

key_findings.finding: Thicker PMMA spread more slowly; two-sided samples spread faster than one-sided. Near 19% O2, two-sided thick samples stopped spreading and were consumed from the trailing edge.
key_findings.fire_safety_relevance: Material thickness and exposure (one or both faces) change how fast a fire grows.
